messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo is a 37-year-old social ministry worker who came to therapy at the urging of his supervisor. For the past year and a half, he has been living in a small apartment on the other side of town from the house he shared with his ex-wife, Elena. The divorce became final eight months ago, but the abuse that ended the marriage happened nearly two years earlier. Late one night, after a community fundraiser where Elena had been drinking heavily, she accused Mateo of hiding money. She shoved him into the bedroom, pinned him face-down on the mattress with her knee in his back, and held his arms behind him so tightly his shoulders ached for days. The smell of cheap whiskey on her breath was suffocating. He could hear the bedroom door slam shut and the lock click. He remembers every second of that night with brutal clarity—the weight on his spine, the sound of her breathing, the way his own voice cracked when he begged her to stop. What haunts him most is not the physical pain but the grief that floods him whenever the memory surfaces: a raw, formless sorrow for the man he used to be.

The smell of alcohol has become a tripwire. A few weeks after the assault, Mateo volunteered at the parish food pantry; a client stepped close, reeking of bourbon, and Mateo’s chest seized. He went rigid, his arms locked at his sides, unable to speak or move until the man walked away. The freeze response is the only thing he can do in that moment—he has learned that trying to push through only makes the shaking worse. Since then, he has stopped taking evening shifts at the pantry and avoids the neighborhood liquor store entirely, even though it means a longer bus ride home. These strategies feel necessary, but he knows they are shrinking his world. The sound of a door opening is almost as bad: at the ministry office, whenever someone slams a filing cabinet or a volunteer lets a door swing shut, Mateo’s head snaps up, his heart hammering. He has started working from a back office with the door wedged open and the lock removed—an ironic choice that he tells himself is for ventilation, though he avoids examining why sitting in a closed room makes his skin crawl.

That vigilance follows him home. Every night, long after his neighbors have gone to sleep, Mateo walks through his apartment checking each window latch and deadbolt. He does it three or four times, even though nothing has ever been disturbed. Darkness amplifies every creak and draft, and he finds it impossible to feel safe after sunset. A sudden movement in his peripheral vision—a stray cat, a curtain shifting in the breeze—makes him flinch as though he is about to be attacked. These startle reactions, in turn, drag the assault back into his mind. The vividness of the memory is undimmed: he can still hear the dry rasp of his own throat against the mattress, the squeak of the bedsprings. Trying to control his emotions only makes the grief worse. At a recent staff meeting, a colleague accidentally knocked a stack of papers off a desk; the sharp slap of paper on tile sent Mateo’s mind straight to that bedroom door slamming shut. He excused himself to the restroom and stood gripping the sink, forcing his breathing to slow, but the auditory recall played itself out behind his eyelids for ten more minutes.

The causal threads tighten into a loop he cannot escape. When he is already on edge from nightmares—he has begun waking at 3 a.m., convinced he smells whiskey—the slightest trigger, like an unexpected hand on his shoulder during a ministry event, sends him straight into a freeze state. And when he freezes, the memory crystallises: he is back under Elena’s weight, unable to move, the grief stabbing through his chest. To break the cycle, he tries to suppress every flicker of emotion, but that vigilance makes him even more sensitive to the triggers. He has started to avoid any situation where someone might touch him, even a friendly pat on the back, which his supervisor noticed and interpreted as coldness. The only place he still feels moderately safe is his own car, doors locked, windows up, radio on low—but even there, the smell of a passing beer truck can ruin an entire drive. Mateo finally walked into therapy because he is afraid of losing his job. He is terrified that one day he will freeze in the middle of a conversation with a parishioner and never find his way back. What he hopes for, though he cannot quite say it aloud, is to someday sit in a room with a closed door and not hear the lock click.
